title: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
summary: Why a CAS that sees the same pointer can still corrupt a lock-free stack, and the four fixes: tagged pointers, double-width CAS or spare bits, LL/SC, and safe reclamation with hazard pointers or epochs.
outcomes: Explain step by step how an A to B to A interleaving makes a Treiber pop corrupt the stack
Trace a tagged-pointer CAS and compute when a b-bit tag can wrap at a given update rate
Choose between 128-bit CAS, spare pointer bits and array indices for storing the tag
Explain why LL/SC avoids ABA in principle and why constrained loops limit it in practice
Compare hazard pointers and epoch-based reclamation by cost and behavior under stalled threads

lessons.title: How a stale CAS corrupts a lock-free stack

blocks.md:
Recall the Treiber stack from the previous course: one shared word, `Top`, points at the first node, and every operation is a retry loop around **compare-and-swap** (CAS). CAS takes an address, an expected value and a new value. It writes the new value only if the location still holds the expected value, and reports whether it did. CAS was introduced on the IBM System/370.

Pop reads `Top` into a local `t`, reads `n = t->next`, then tries `CAS(&Top, t, n)`. If another thread changed `Top` in between, the CAS fails and the loop retries.

blocks.caption: The naive pop. It looks correct, and under most interleavings it is.

blocks.md:
The hidden assumption is in the CAS. It answers "does `Top` hold the same *value* I read?", not "has nobody touched `Top` since I read it?". Those questions differ when a value can leave and come back.

That is the **ABA problem**, as Michael and Scott define it: a thread reads value A from a shared location, other threads change it to B and then back to A, and the first thread's CAS succeeds when it should not. With pointers, "back to A" happens whenever a node's memory is reused at the same address: pushed again from a free list, or handed out again by the allocator after a free.

blocks.prompt: The stack is Top, A, B, C. Thread T1 reads t = A and n = B, then stalls. Thread T2 pops A, pops B, and pushes A back (reusing node A). T1 wakes up and runs CAS(&Top, A, B). Does it succeed, and what does the stack look like afterwards?
blocks.reveal: It **succeeds**, because `Top` holds A again. T1 installs B as the new top. But B is no longer on the stack: T2 popped it and still owns it. The stack becomes Top, B, C. Node A, which T2 had legitimately pushed, is now unreachable, and node B is on the stack while T2 is also using it. Nothing crashed; the structure is silently wrong.

blocks.title: The A to B to A interleaving on a Treiber stack

scenes.caption: Initial stack Top, A, B, C. T1 has read t = A and n = B and is about to CAS, but it gets descheduled.
T2 pops A: its CAS moves Top from A to B. Node A now belongs to T2 (row below = off the stack).
T2 pops B as well. Top now points at C. Both A and B are off the stack.
T2 pushes node A again (same address, new contents), so A.next = C and Top = A. The value in Top is back to A.
T1 resumes. CAS(&Top, A, B) compares only the value, sees A, and succeeds. Top now points at B, which T2 still owns, and A is lost.

blocks.md:
Notice what the bug needs: T1 must stall in a window of a few instructions, between reading `t->next` and its CAS, while other threads pop at least twice and recycle the very address T1 holds. That is why ABA is rare in tests and real in production, where threads get preempted at arbitrary instructions.

Also notice which operation is at risk. Michael's hazard pointer paper points out that in this stack only **pop's** CAS is ABA-prone. Push writes `node->next` into a node the pushing thread owns, so a stale `Top` just makes its CAS fail or link correctly.

CAS checks *equality of value*, not *absence of change*. Any algorithm that reads a pointer, computes from what it points to, and then CASes on that pointer is wrong if the pointed-to node can be recycled in between.

blocks.question: In the naive pop, which step makes the algorithm ABA-prone?
options: Reading Top with an atomic load instead of a lock
Using the successor n, read from t before the CAS, as the new value of a CAS that only compares t
Calling compare_exchange_weak, which can fail spuriously
Returning t to the caller after the CAS
blocks.explain: The CAS validates only that Top still equals t. The value n was computed from t's contents earlier and may be stale if t was popped and pushed back. Spurious failures of the weak form just cause a retry; they never cause a wrong success.

blocks.question: Suppose your stack never frees or reuses a popped node (it just leaks them). Can the interleaving above still corrupt it?
options: Yes, because CAS always compares values
Yes, because Top can wrap around
No, because Top can hold address A again only if node A is pushed again, which never happens
blocks.explain: After A is popped, the only way Top can equal A again is to push the node at address A. With no reuse, a stale CAS expecting A always fails. This is the observation behind safe memory reclamation in the last lesson. Leaking is not a real solution, but it shows that reuse is the trigger.

lessons.title: Tagged pointers: a version counter beside the pointer

blocks.md:
The oldest fix comes from IBM's System/370 documentation, which is also where Michael says ABA was first reported. Make the shared word a pair, **{pointer, tag}**, where the tag is a counter. Michael and Scott describe the rule: always read the counter together with the pointer, compare both in the CAS, and increment the counter in every successful CAS.

Now "the same value" means "the same pointer *and* the same version". A recycled address comes back with a larger tag, so the stale CAS fails.

blocks.caption: Tagged pop. Push also writes {node, old.tag + 1}. compare_exchange compares the whole 16-byte object.

blocks.title: Replaying the same interleaving with a tag

scenes.caption: T1 reads Top = {A, 0} and n = B, then stalls. Its CAS will expect exactly {A, 0}.
T2 pops A. Its successful CAS writes {B, 1}: the tag goes up by one.
T2 pops B: Top = {C, 2}.
T2 pushes node A again. The pointer is back to A, but the push CAS also bumped the tag: Top = {A, 3}.
T1 resumes and runs CAS(Top, {A, 0}, {B, 1}). Pointers match, tags do not (0 vs 3), so the CAS fails. Nothing is corrupted.
The failed CAS reloads {A, 3}. T1 rereads n = C and CASes to {C, 4}, correctly popping A.

blocks.caption: p is the pointer, g the tag, k the number of successful CASes since the read, b the tag width. A stale CAS can only succeed if k is a multiple of 2^b.

blocks.md: The tag does not need to be unique forever. It only needs to differ from the value a stalled thread is holding. With a $b$-bit tag, that fails only if exactly a multiple of $2^b$ successful updates happen while the thread is stalled *and* the same pointer is on top again. Michael and Scott are careful here: counters do "not guarantee that the ABA problem will not occur, but it makes it extremely unlikely". The next lesson puts numbers on "extremely".

A tag protects the CAS, not the read before it. In the pop above, `old.ptr->next` is read from a node that may already have been popped by someone else. That is safe only if popped nodes stay mapped and readable, for example on a type-stable free list (nodes reused only as nodes, never freed). Michael notes that the IBM tag method "hinders memory reclamation for arbitrary reuse": you cannot return such nodes to the OS while a thread may still dereference them.
Tagged pointer = pointer plus a counter compared and swapped as one unit, bumped on every successful CAS. It turns "same value" into "same value and same version".

blocks.question: A thread reads Top = {A, 7} and stalls. Meanwhile other threads perform 5 successful CASes, and the last one leaves node A on top again. What does the stalled thread's CAS see, and what happens?
options: {A, 12}: it fails, then reloads and retries
{A, 7}: it succeeds, because the pointer matches
{A, 8}: it fails, because only pushes bump the tag
blocks.explain: Every successful CAS bumps the tag, so after 5 of them the word holds {A, 12}. The expected {A, 7} no longer matches, the CAS fails, and compare_exchange reloads the current {A, 12} for the retry.

blocks.question: Spot the bug: a developer stores the pointer and the tag in two separate std::atomic variables, loads them one after the other, and uses a 16-byte CAS only at the end. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: the final CAS compares both fields anyway
The tag will overflow faster
The two loads can pair an old pointer with a newer tag, so the snapshot may describe no state that ever existed
blocks.explain: Michael and Scott require the counter to be read together with the pointer. Two separate loads can interleave with updates, giving a mixed pair. Besides, a CAS can only cover one memory location, so pointer and tag must live in the same atomic word to be compared together at all.

lessons.title: Finding room for the tag: wide CAS, spare bits, indices

blocks.md: The tag must be compared in the same atomic instruction as the pointer, so it has to live in the same machine word. On a 64-bit machine a pointer already fills a word. Michael and Scott list the two classic answers: use a **double-word CAS**, or replace pointers with **array indices** small enough to share a word with a counter. A third, common in practice, is to hide the tag in pointer bits the hardware does not use.

**Double-width CAS.** On x86-64, `LOCK CMPXCHG16B` compares the 16-byte memory operand with RDX:RAX and, if equal, stores RCX:RBX; otherwise it loads the memory into RDX:RAX. The operand must be 16-byte aligned. This gives a full 64-bit pointer plus a 64-bit tag. In C++, a 16-byte `std::atomic` may or may not compile to this instruction depending on compiler and flags, so check `is_lock_free()` rather than assuming.

**Array indices.** Allocate nodes from a fixed array and link them by 32-bit index. A 32-bit index plus a 32-bit counter fit in one 64-bit word, so an ordinary 64-bit CAS suffices.

**Spare pointer bits.** The Linux x86-64 memory map says the architecture defines 64-bit virtual addresses, but implementations support 48 or 57 bits, and the bits above are copies of the top implemented bit. With 4-level paging, user space is the lowest 128 TB (addresses below $2^{47}$), so the top 16 bits of a user pointer are zero. Boost.Lockfree's compressed `tagged_ptr` uses exactly this: a 16-bit tag in the top bits and the mask `0xffffffffffff` (48 bits) for the pointer. Alignment frees low bits too: a 16-byte aligned node always has 4 zero low bits.

blocks.title: Packing a tag into a 64-bit user pointer (one cell = 4 bits)

scenes.caption: A 16-byte aligned user pointer, 0x7f3a5c1e40a0, under 4-level paging. The top 4 hex digits (16 bits) are always zero for user space.
Store tag 3 in the top 16 bits. The word is now 0x00037f3a5c1e40a0. One 64-bit CAS compares pointer and tag together.
Before dereferencing, mask with 0xffffffffffff to recover the pointer. The low hex digit is always 0 here because the node is 16-byte aligned: 4 more spare bits.
Tag 0xffff plus one wraps to 0x0000. After 65,536 successful CASes the word can repeat exactly.
With 5-level paging, user space can grow to 56 bits. A pointer like 0x00ab12cd5c1e40a0 uses bits the tag scheme assumed were free; only the top 8 remain.

blocks.md: Spare-bit tricks depend on the address space. The kernel's 5-level paging notes say some JIT compilers store information in high pointer bits, which collides with valid pointers once 56-bit addresses exist. So Linux does not hand out user addresses above 47 bits unless a program asks with a high `mmap` hint. A library that packs a 16-bit tag silently breaks in a process that opts in.

**How fast does a tag wrap?** Use a simple model: the contended word sees $r$ successful CASes per second. A $b$-bit tag returns to the same value every $2^b / r$ seconds. A stalled thread is fooled only if it sleeps through an exact multiple of that period and finds the same pointer on top, but the period tells you how long a stall must be before that is even possible.

blocks.caption: r = 10 million successful CASes per second is an assumed, heavily contended rate for illustration.

blocks.prompt: Keep r = 10 million CASes per second. How long until a 32-bit tag wraps? And a 64-bit tag?
blocks.reveal: 32-bit: $2^{32} / 10^7 \approx 429.5$ s, about 7.2 minutes. 64-bit: $2^{64} / 10^7 \approx 1.84 \times 10^{12}$ s, roughly 58,000 years. A 16-bit tag wraps in 6.6 ms, which is within reach of an ordinary preemption or page fault. That is why 128-bit CAS with a full 64-bit tag is the conservative choice.

blocks.title: Time until a b-bit tag repeats

scenes.caption: At 10 million CASes per second, a 16-bit tag repeats every 6.6 ms. A thread preempted for longer could in principle see its old tag again.
32 bits stretch that to about 7 minutes, still conceivable for a stopped or swapped-out thread.
A 64-bit tag in a 128-bit CAS needs about 58,000 years at the same rate. Drag the slider to see how each bit doubles the period.

blocks.question: You build a lock-free stack for a long-running x86-64 Linux server that may map memory above 47 bits and runs millions of operations per second. Which tagging scheme fits best?
options: 16-bit tag in the top pointer bits, as in a compressed tagged_ptr
A 4-bit tag in the low alignment bits
No tag: ABA is too rare to matter
A 64-bit tag beside a full pointer, swapped with CMPXCHG16B on a 16-byte aligned word
blocks.explain: High bits may hold real address bits once the process uses addresses above 47 bits, and a 4-bit or 16-bit tag wraps within microseconds to tens of milliseconds at millions of CASes per second. A full 64-bit tag in a double-width CAS keeps all pointer bits and makes wraparound practically impossible.

blocks.question: Your nodes come from a pool of at most 4 billion entries. Which layout lets you avoid both double-width CAS and spare pointer bits?
options: 32-bit array index and 32-bit tag in one 64-bit word
64-bit pointer and 64-bit tag
48-bit pointer and 16-bit tag
blocks.explain: This is the array-index option from Michael and Scott: an index into a node array needs only 32 bits for up to 2^32 nodes, leaving 32 bits for the counter, and an ordinary 64-bit CAS covers both.

lessons.title: LL/SC: watching the location instead of its value

blocks.md:
Some architectures offer a different primitive pair: **load-linked / store-conditional** (LL/SC). LL reads a location and starts watching it. SC writes a new value only if no other thread has written the location since the LL, and reports success or failure. On RISC-V these are `lr.d` and `sc.d`: LR registers a *reservation set* covering the loaded bytes, and an SC may succeed only if no store from another hart (RISC-V's word for a hardware thread) to that set can be observed between the LR and the SC. SC writes 0 to its result register on success and a nonzero value on failure.

The key difference from CAS: SC fails on *any* intervening write, even one that restores the old value.

blocks.title: The same A to B to A, seen by LL/SC

scenes.caption: T1 executes LR on Top and gets A. The hardware records a reservation on the bytes of Top.
T2 pops A: a store to Top. That store breaks T1's reservation, whatever value it writes.
T2 pops B and pushes A back. Top's value is A again, exactly as T1 saw it.
T1 attempts SC. A CAS expecting A would succeed here; the SC fails because Top was written. T1 retries with fresh values.

blocks.md: The RISC-V designers cite this directly: they chose LR/SC over CAS partly because "CAS suffers from the ABA problem, which LR/SC avoids because it monitors all writes to the address". They also note the alternative, a double-wide CAS with a counter, needs an instruction that reads five registers and writes two.

So why is ABA still a topic? Because real LL/SC is restricted. Michael's 2004 paper notes that no LL/SC machine of the time (Alpha, MIPS, PowerPC) allowed nesting, most prohibited any memory access between LL and SC, and all could fail spuriously. RISC-V spells out a modern version: only a **constrained** LR/SC loop is guaranteed to eventually succeed. It must be at most 16 instructions, and the code between LR and SC may not contain loads, stores, backward jumps or several other instruction kinds. Unconstrained sequences "might never succeed" on some implementations.

blocks.code:
# RV64 Treiber pop with LR/SC. a0 = ⊤ Node.next at offset 0.
retry:
    lr.d   t0, (a0)        # t = top, reserve the top word
    beqz   t0, empty
    ld     t1, 0(t0)       # n = t->next  (a load between LR and SC)
    sc.d   t2, t1, (a0)    # top = n only if no store hit the reservation
    bnez   t2, retry       # nonzero = SC failed
    mv     a0, t0          # return t
    ret
empty:
    li     a0, 0
    ret
blocks.caption: ABA-free in principle, but the ld between lr.d and sc.d makes this an unconstrained sequence with no forward-progress guarantee.

blocks.md: Portable C and C++ code does not get LL/SC semantics. `compare_exchange` is defined as a value comparison; on an LL/SC machine the compiler builds it from an LL/SC loop that starts *after* your earlier plain load of `top`. The window where ABA strikes (between that load and the CAS) is outside the reservation, so ABA is back.
LL/SC detects *writes*, so it is immune to A to B to A in principle. In practice the pop needs a load between LL and SC, which hardware does not guarantee to support, and languages expose CAS anyway.

blocks.question: T1 does LR on Top and reads A. T2 then stores A into Top (the same value it already held). What happens to T1's SC?
options: It succeeds, since the value never changed
It succeeds only if T2's store was atomic
It may not succeed: a store by another hart to the reservation set, even of the same value, means the SC fails
blocks.explain: The SC condition is about stores, not values: it may succeed only if no store from another hart to the reservation set occurred between LR and SC. That is precisely what defeats ABA.

blocks.question: Why can't a portable lock-free stack on RISC-V simply rely on LR/SC to avoid ABA in pop?
options: RISC-V has no LR/SC instructions on RV64
Pop must load t->next between LR and SC, which falls outside a constrained loop, so eventual success is not guaranteed
SC never fails, so it behaves exactly like CAS
blocks.explain: Constrained LR/SC loops forbid loads between LR and SC. The pop's dependent load makes the loop unconstrained, and the spec says such sequences might never succeed on some implementations, so portable code needs a fallback.

lessons.title: Hazard pointers and epochs: stop reuse while anyone looks

blocks.md:
Lesson 1 showed the trigger: node A was **reused** while T1 still held its address. Michael's hazard pointer paper makes this the general fix: if no node can be reused while some thread may still use its address, pointer ABA from reuse cannot happen, and memory can be freed to the OS safely. Garbage collection gives this for free; hazard pointers and epochs give it in C, C++ and Rust.

Both schemes split removal into two steps. **Retire**: unlink the node so no new thread can find it. **Reclaim**: free it later, once no thread can still be holding it.

**Hazard pointers.** Each thread owns a few (typically one or two) shared pointer slots that only it writes and everyone reads. Before using a node it *announces* the node's address in a slot, then *re-checks* that the node is still reachable. A retiring thread puts nodes on a private list; once it holds R of them, it scans every thread's slots and frees only the nodes nobody has announced.

blocks.caption: Treiber pop with one hazard pointer, following Michael's construction (announce, validate, use). No tag needed.

nodes.label:
T3 retired list
A, B, C

scenes.caption: T1 announced A in its slot and is about to read A's next. T3 has retired A, B and C, reaching its threshold R, so it scans.
Stage 1: T3 reads every slot and collects the non-null ones into a local set, plist = {A}.
Stage 2: each retired node is looked up in plist. B and C are unprotected and freed; A stays on T3's list for a later scan.
Because A cannot be reused while T1's slot holds it, Top can never show A again under T1's feet. T1's CAS on A is safe without any tag.

blocks.tex: H = N K, \qquad R = H + \Omega(H), \qquad \text{retired but not yet reusable} \le N R
blocks.caption: Michael's bounds: N threads with K slots each. Example: N = 4, K = 1 gives H = 4; choosing R = 2H = 8 bounds unreclaimed nodes by 32, even if threads stall.

blocks.md: **Epoch-based reclamation**, described by Fraser, avoids the per-access announcement. A global epoch counter advances; each thread notes the epoch when it starts an operation. Retired nodes go into a limbo list tagged with the current epoch. When every thread currently inside an operation has seen the current epoch, the list from **two** epochs ago can be freed, so three lists suffice. Rust's `crossbeam-epoch` works this way: `pin()` a thread before loading, and `defer` destruction until the epoch has advanced enough.

blocks.title: Epochs advance only when every active thread catches up (simplified)

scenes.caption: Epoch 0. Every operation records the epoch it saw. Nodes retired now go to limbo list 0.
All active threads have seen epoch 0, so the epoch moves to 1. Threads in epoch 1 may still hold nodes from list 0, so it is not freed yet.
At epoch 2, nobody can still hold a node retired in epoch 0: limbo list 0 is freed and recycled for new garbage.
T3 stalls inside an operation and never sees a newer epoch. The epoch stops advancing, so limbo lists stop being freed and garbage grows without bound.

blocks.md: That last scene is the tradeoff Fraser states plainly: epoch reclamation is "not strictly lock-free", because a thread stalled mid-operation stops reclamation for everyone. Hazard pointers bound garbage even when threads stall, but every protected access pays for an announcement that must be visible to other processors before use, which Fraser identifies as a costly memory barrier. Tagged pointers need neither, but they keep nodes in type-stable memory forever.

"Garbage collection solves ABA" is a common misconception that Michael calls out. GC prevents ABA caused by *reuse*, but if a program moves the same nodes back and forth between two lock-free stacks, a node can leave and return to the same position with perfect GC. Ask whether the algorithm is ABA-safe under GC first; only then do hazard pointers or epochs make it ABA-safe without GC.

Choose by failure mode. Tagged pointers: cheap, but need wide CAS or spare bits and type-stable nodes. LL/SC: ABA-free in principle, rarely usable directly. Hazard pointers: bounded garbage under stalls, cost per access. Epochs: cheapest per access, but one stalled thread blocks all reclamation.

blocks.question: A thread can be suspended for minutes inside a data structure operation (for example, it is stopped by a debugger or swapped out). You must keep memory bounded. Which scheme fits?
options: Hazard pointers, because a stalled thread can block reclamation of only the nodes it has announced
Epoch-based reclamation, because it has the lowest per-access cost
A 16-bit tagged pointer with nodes freed immediately
blocks.explain: Michael proves at most N times R retired nodes stay unreclaimed regardless of stalls. Epochs stop advancing while the stalled thread sits in a critical region, so all garbage is retained. Freeing tagged nodes immediately lets the stale read of next touch freed memory, and 16-bit tags can wrap.

blocks.question: In the hazard pointer pop, a developer removes the line that re-checks top.load() != t after announcing t. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, the announcement alone protects t
The CAS will always fail
Between reading t and announcing it, t may have been popped, retired and freed by a scan that did not see the announcement, so reading t->next touches freed memory
blocks.explain: Michael's condition requires the hazard pointer to cover the node from a time when it was still reachable. The re-check proves t was still on the stack after the announcement was visible, so any later scan must see it. Without it, a retire and scan can slip in before the announcement.
